turns.label: turn 1 — differential
detected_by_validator:
Dens evaginatus with pulp horn extension
*Fits because:* Tooth #20 is the mandibular left second premolar — the single most frequently reported tooth for dens evaginatus.

The patient is 20 years old and of Asian origin, precisely the demographic and age group in which this anomaly classically presents with pulp necrosis: the evaginated tubercle fractures or abrades during occlusal function in the early teens
CBCT is indicated when conventional imaging is insufficient to characterise the cause of periapical pathology [[PMID:AAE-PS-cbct]].

turns.label: turn 2 — prevention
detected_by_validator: 1. **Reduce occlusal contact on the tubercle** — selective equilibration to eliminate traumatic occlusal loading on the cusp.
This is the single most impactful step; gradual attrition of an unloaded tubercle allows reparative/secondary dentine to progressively wall off the pulp horn before exposure occurs.

3. **Gradual elective reduction of the tubercle over multiple visits** — performed in small increments (0.5 mm per visit) with 6–8 week intervals, allowing secondary dentine deposition to track ahead of the reduction.
Calcium hydroxide or MTA liner placement after each reduction step is advocated in the literature for deeper reductions.

4. **Monitor with cold test and periapical radiographs every 6 months** — pulp canal obliteration on sequential films is a reassuring sign of active reparative dentine formation and continued vitality.
Screen the entire mouth for DE — mandibular second premolars are the classic site but mandibular first premolars and, occasionally, maxillary premolars can also be affected.
Patient education is critical — the patient must understand not to bite hard foods (nuts, ice, hard crusts) that could abruptly fracture the remaining tubercle on any unmanaged DE tooth.
